Shri V. C. Padmanabhan belonged to the coastal fishing village of Valapad in Malabar district of the erstwhile Madras 
Presidency. He was committed to uplifting the economically weaker sections of the society, particularly the farmers, 
fishermen and agricultural laborers in his community. In 1949, he decided to help the people of his village by setting 
up his own small business of providing loans against the security of jewelry at affordable rates. Thus, began the 
story of Manappuram Finance Limited (MAFIL).
Over the years and decades, the Company has won the trust of millions of customers and has played a pivotal role in 
bringing underprivileged people into the fold of organized lending.
Driven by Shri Padmanabhan’s values of trust and integrity, Manappuram Finance Limited has transformed itself 
into a full-fledged and well-diversified non-banking financial company (NBFC) that will continue to exceed customer 
expectations and help them fulfill their aspirations. Our core strengths of customer-centricity, stakeholder integrity 
and quick adoption of top-notch technology for seamless operations will help us stay ahead of the curve.

About Us
Backed by a legacy of 75+ years, Manappuram Finance Limited (Manappuram) has 
evolved from a modest Kerala-based venture to one of India’s leading and trusted 
non-banking financial companies (NBFCs). Rooted in a commitment to expanding 
formal credit access to underbanked segments, we offer accessible, secure and 
sustainable financial solutions, empowering millions across India’s semi-urban and 
rural regions to realize their financial aspirations.
As India’s second-largest gold loan NBFC, we leverage our 
extensive branch network to offer a comprehensive financial 
solutions portfolio, including gold loans to microfinance (through 
Asirvad), vehicle and equipment finance, home loans to MSME 
lending and insurance, to serve the evolving financial needs of 
our customers across 25 States and 3 Union Territories. 
Guided by visionary leadership, strategic partnerships and 
supported by dedicated team capabilities, we maintain an 
unwavering focus on tech-led innovation, operational excellence 
and customer centricity, transforming the lending experience. 
Industry-best governance practices, a robust capital position, 
financial prudence and disciplined execution continue to 
reinforce stakeholder trust, enabling responsible growth and 
scalability within India’s evolving financial services landscape.

to benefit immensely from its deep expertise in financial services 
in India. Supported by our robust platform, this partnership is

services, further strengthening our journey towards becoming a 
diversified financial solutions provider.

Dear Stakeholders,
FY 2025-26 has been a year that tested 
our foundations and found them solid. 
Manappuram demonstrated, once again, 
that institutions built to last do not 
merely survive adversity; they convert 
it into competitive advantage. We began 
the year carrying the weight of sectoral 
headwinds in microfinance and the 
after-effects of elevated provisioning 
in FY 2024-25. We end it with our 
gold loan franchise surging to historic 
highs, our consolidated AUM crossing 
` 63,798 Crores, up 48.3% YoY. This is 
what purposeful growth looks like: not 
the pursuit of scale at any cost, but the 
compounding of trust, discipline and 
institutional strength over time.
A Year Defined by the Gold 
Franchise
The gold loan business has always been 
the bedrock of Manappuram Finance 
Limited. In FY 2025-26, it became our 
engine of renaissance and the clearest 
expression of what it means to be poised 
to lead. Consolidated gold loan AUM 
reached ` 50,953 Crores by the close 
of the year, almost doubling YoY with a 
growth of 99.1%. Standalone gold loan 
AUM stood at ` 48,814 Crores, up 98% 
YoY. This extraordinary performance was 
underpinned by sustained gold price 
appreciation, disciplined loan-to-value 
(LTV) governance, with the LTV remaining 
stable at 57% and the deepening reach 
of our online gold loan (OGL) platform 
across our network of 3,524 gold loan 
branches. 
What makes this growth especially 
significant is its quality. It was not 
pursued at the cost of governance. 
Our underwriting standards remained 
intact, our auction discipline held firm 
and our customer trust, earned over 
decades of safekeeping nearly 63 
metric tons of household gold jewelry 
on behalf of 2.7 Million active customers, 
continued to grow. This is what growth 
with purpose means at Manappuram: 
expanding our reach without 
compromising the values that make 
that reach meaningful. This trust is our 
most durable asset, and we guard it with 
unwavering commitment.
Navigating the Regulatory 
Landscape
FY 2025-26 was a year of heightened 
regulatory engagement for the gold 
lending sector. The Reserve Bank of 
India’s evolving guidelines on gold 
loans demanded careful attention and 
we approached this with the seriousness 
it deserved. Progress with prudence 
has never been a mere slogan for us; it 
describes how we have always engaged 
with regulation: not as a constraint to 
be managed, but as a framework that 
defines the boundaries of sustainable 
conduct. Our decades of experience in 
appraisal, custodial management and 
LTV discipline positioned us well to adapt 
swiftly and substantively. Our CRAR at 
the close of FY 2025-26 stood at 21.3%, 
well above regulatory requirements, a 
testament to our capital adequacy and 
long-term financial soundness.
We welcome the regulatory direction 
towards greater transparency in gold 
lending. As one of the largest listed 
gold loan NBFCs in India and a pioneer 
in process innovation in this segment, 
we believe that higher standards serve 
both the industry and the customer. 
Manappuram has consistently been 
ahead of the curve in this regard, from 
the cellular vaulting mechanism to the 
online gold loan product and we intend 
to remain so.
Built to Last, Poised 
to Lead

Microfinance: From Consolidation 
to Growth
Our subsidiary Asirvad Micro Finance 
Limited continued its recovery journey 
in FY 2025-26. Following the sectoral 
stress of the previous year, we adopted 
a deliberately cautious posture, 
prioritizing asset quality over volume, 
strengthening collections and calibrating 
fresh disbursements against real 
improvements in borrower leverage. 
This was prudence in practice: accepting 
near-term compression in the interest 
of long-term portfolio health. By the 
fourth quarter, the microfinance book 
had begun to show stabilization, with 
AUM at ` 4,636 Crores and meaningful 
improvement in portfolio hygiene metrics. 
We are encouraged by these early signs, 
but we remain watchful. Recovery in 
microfinance is a marathon, not a sprint 
and we shall pursue it with discipline.
Financial Performance: A Full-Year 
View 
On a consolidated basis, FY 2025-26 
revenue stood at ` 9,509 Crores and 
PAT at ` 993 Crores, with a Return on 
Average Assets of 2.0%. These full-year 
figures reflect the weight of elevated 
provisioning earlier in the year, 
particularly in non-gold segments. 
However, the trajectory through the 
year tells a more encouraging story. 
Q4 FY 2025-26 delivered consolidated 
PAT of ` 405 Crores, representing a 70% 
sequential improvement, driven by gold 
loan momentum, NIM recovery and 
moderation in credit costs. Our Net Worth 
grew 29.1% YoY to ` 16,051 Crores, 
reflecting the accretion of capital and the 
confidence of our strategic investor.
The Board declared quarterly 
dividends totaling ` 2 per share across 
FY 2025-26, reaffirming our commitment 
to shareholder returns even as we 
reinvested for growth. Our credit ratings 
remain strong and continue to underpin 
our access to diversified, cost-effective 
funding. Consolidated cost of borrowing 
stood at 8.80% in Q4 FY 2025-26, a 
reflection of both market conditions and 
our strong credit standing. These numbers 
are not merely the outcome of a single 
year’s effort; they are the product of 
decades of institutional discipline, quietly 
compounding.
Technology and Digital 
Transformation 
The digital transformation of Manappuram 
is not a headline ambition; it is a daily 
operational reality. Our OGL platform 
and MACOM, our internal technology 
subsidiary, collectively represent 
a deepening investment in making 
financial services faster, safer and 
more accessible for underbanked 
customers. In FY 2025-26, we expanded 
our network across all business lines, 
with an employee strength of over 
42,000 on a consolidated basis, even 
as we scaled our digital touchpoints 
significantly. We have also reinforced our 
cybersecurity measures in recognition of 
the risks that accompany digital scale.
We see technology not as a substitute for 
our branch network and the human trust 
it embodies, but as its amplifier. The future 
of gold lending in India is a hybrid model, 
branch presence combined with digital 
convenience, and Manappuram is well 
positioned to lead this transformation.
The Bain Capital Partnership
A landmark development of FY 2025-26 
has been the induction of Bain Capital 
as a strategic investor. This represents 
a significant vote of confidence in the 
Manappuram story: our track record, our 
governance culture, our market position 
and our long-term growth potential. It is 
also an affirmation of something deeper: 
that investors looking for institutions 
poised to lead, not just for a quarter, 
but for a decade, find in Manappuram a 
compelling proposition. Beyond capital, 
this partnership brings global strategic 
perspective and a shared commitment 
to building a world-class, customer-first 
financial institution. We look forward to 
leveraging this relationship as we enter 
the next phase of our evolution.
Looking Ahead
As we step into FY 2026-27, our priorities 
are clear. We will continue to strengthen 
the gold loan franchise by deepening 
penetration, improving digital adoption 
and defending our leadership position. 
We will pursue the full recovery and 
eventual re-scaling of the microfinance 
business, guided by data and customer 
outcomes rather than volume targets. 
We will grow our secured lending verticals, 
including housing finance, equipment 
finance and MSME lending, with the 
same discipline that defines our gold 
loan operations. We will also continue to 
invest in our people, our technology and 
our governance frameworks, because 
these are the foundations on which 
sustainable growth is built.
India’s long-term macroeconomic 
trajectory remains compelling. 
Rising financial inclusion, expanding 
credit penetration and the enduring 
relevance of gold as collateral in Indian 
households create a structural tailwind 
for Manappuram’s core proposition. 
We intend to convert that tailwind into 
lasting value by growing with purpose, 
progressing with prudence and leading 
with the confidence that comes from 
knowing what we are built of.
A Note of Gratitude
I wish to express my deep gratitude to 
our Board of Directors for their counsel 
and governance, to our 42,000-strong 
workforce for their commitment through 
a demanding year and to our customers 
for the trust they continue to repose 
in us. To our Shareholders, thank you 
for your patience and your belief in the 
long-term Manappuram story. And to 
our Regulators, whose guidance keeps 
us aligned with the broader public good, 
we remain committed to earning and 
maintaining your confidence.
The institution we are building measures 
its success not just by the numbers it 
delivers, but by the lives it touches and 
the trust it sustains. Built to last. Poised to 
lead. That is not merely a statement of 
ambition; it is a description of who we 
already are, and a commitment to who 
we will continue to become.
With humility and determination,

reinforcing our core mission of providing accessible and inclusive credit solutions to

Management Discussion and Analysis
Manappuram Finance Limited: An Overview
Manappuram Finance Limited (hereafter referred to as “MAFIL” 
or “the Company”) is a leading non-banking financial company 
(NBFC) in India, with its Registered office and corporate 
headquarters located in Valapad, Thrissur. Over the years, the 
Company has transformed into a well-diversified financial 
services institution, with a strong national presence. The Company 
has been expanding rapidly to extend its offerings beyond gold 
loans, including microfinance, vehicle finance, affordable housing 
finance, loan against properties and MSME lending, positioning 
it to meet the diverse financial needs of a wide customer base.
With its ranking as the second-largest gold loan NBFC in India, 
MAFIL enjoys a strong brand identity and consumer confidence 
across multiple regions. The strong focus on innovation 
enables the Company to introduce industry-leading solutions 
in gold financing, including early rollout of its Online Gold Loan 
(OGL), supported by a secured cellular vaulting framework. 
This digital solution provides customers with gold-backed 
credit access, offering 24x7 location-independent access and 
simplified documentation. The Company’s multilingual mobile 
application complements this, improving accessibility and 
inclusivity by serving customers across multiple socio-economic 
segments, strengthening its position as a technology-led and 
customer-focused financial services provider.
Additionally, the Company operates through its diversified 
subsidiaries, extending its reach in the Indian financial 
services industry.
Asirvad Microfinance Limited (AMFL), acquired by MAFIL in 2015, 
is a Non-Banking Financial Company-Micro Finance Institution 
(NBFC-MFI), providing microfinance solutions to women from 
economically weaker households, with its diversified portfolio 
comprising income-generation loans, gold loan, product loans 
and MSME financing.
Manappuram Home Finance Limited (MAHOFIN): MAHOFIN 
emphasizes the affordable housing industry, providing lending for 
home construction, home improvement and selected commercial 
property requirements to retail borrowers.
Manappuram Insurance Brokers Limited (MAIBRO): MAIBRO 
operates as the insurance brokerage firm of MAFIL, enabling 
the distribution of life and general insurance solutions through 
established partnerships with prominent insurance companies.
Manappuram Comptech and Consultants Limited (MACOM): 
MACOM focuses on providing technology support services, 
with capabilities spanning application development for digital 
personal lending and loan management systems.
Economic Overview
Global Economy
The global economy in FY 2025-26 operated within a complex 
and increasingly uncertain macroeconomic environment, 
marked by trade restrictions, policy uncertainty and persistent 
geopolitical tensions. Ongoing conflicts in Eastern Europe and 
the Middle East, including the Russia-Ukraine war, continued 
to disrupt global supply chains, energy markets and investor 
sentiment, leading to periodic volatility in commodity prices and 
financial conditions. At the same time, rising tariffs, changing 
trade arrangements and increasing geo-economic fragmentation 
added to uncertainty in global trade and investment flows.
Despite these headwinds, global economic activity remained 
resilient during the year, supported by stable labor markets, 
continued fiscal support and technology-led investments, 
particularly in Artificial Intelligence (AI). Economies also adapted 
through diversified trade routes, enhanced energy security 
measures and supply chain realignment, which contributed to 
a relatively stable recovery. As a result, global growth stood at 
3.4% in CY 2025, compared to 3.3% in CY 2024.
Advanced economies recorded growth of 1.9% in CY 2025, 
supported by relatively stable labor markets, easing financial 
conditions and recovering demand. Meanwhile, Emerging Market 
and Developing Economies (EMDEs) expanded by 4.4%, driven 
by resilient domestic consumption, improving activity across 
manufacturing and services, and continued infrastructure 
investments in key Asian economies.
Global headline inflation moderated to 4.1% in CY 2025, reflecting 
easing supply-side pressures and the impact of earlier monetary 
tightening measures. However, inflation trends remained uneven 
across regions, with inflation remaining higher in the United 
States while remaining relatively subdued in several other major 
economies.

Outlook
As CY 2026 unfolds, the global economy faces renewed 
uncertainty, largely driven by escalating tensions in West 
Asia and disruptions across critical energy transit routes. 
Rising concerns around the supply of oil, LNG, LPG and fertilizers 
have intensified risks related to energy security, inflationary 
pressures and supply chain stability. Against this backdrop, 
global growth is projected to moderate to 3.1% in CY 2026 before 
improving marginally to 3.2% in CY 2027.
However, improving diplomatic efforts, strategic energy 
diversification and stronger regional co-operation are expected 
to gradually ease these pressures. This is likely to support supply 
chain stability, moderate inflation, and foster a more balanced 
and resilient global economic recovery.
Advanced economies are expected to grow at 1.8% in CY 
2026, while emerging market and developing economies are 
projected to expand by 3.9%, supported by domestic demand and 
continued infrastructure spending. Growth in the United States 
(U.S.) remains a key driver of the global outlook, with the IMF 
raising the U.S. forecast and GDP projected to grow by about 
2.3% in CY 2026 and 2.1% in CY 2027.
Central banks are expected to remain cautious, while governments 
continue to focus on fiscal discipline, targeted policy support and 
strengthening supply chain resilience amid the evolving global 
economic landscape.
Indian Economy
The Indian economy remained one of the fastest-growing major 
economies in FY 2025-26, supported by resilient domestic 
demand, infrastructure-led investment and policy reforms. 
According to the Provisional Estimates released by the Ministry 
of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), real GDP 
grew by 7.7% during the year, while real Gross Value Added 
(GVA) increased by 7.9% to ` 294.91 Lakh Crore.
The services sector remained the key growth driver, while 
manufacturing witnessed continued improvement supported 
by government-led production initiatives and infrastructure 
spending. India continues to remain among the world’s largest 
economies, currently ranking as the sixth-largest economy 
globally in nominal GDP terms as per the IMF. Private consumption 
and investment remained the primary drivers of economic growth. 
Structural reforms such as GST, Production Linked Incentive (PLI) 
schemes, and Make in India 2.0 continue to improve formalization, 
manufacturing competitiveness and ease of doing business, 
while strengthening India’s position within global supply chains. 
The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) grew by 4.1% year-on-
year in March 2026, driven by growth in the manufacturing 
(4.3%) and mining (5.5%) sectors. The continued expansion in 
industrial activity, supported by healthy demand conditions and 
ongoing investments, augurs well for the manufacturing sector 
and provides a favorable environment for future growth.
The conflict in West Asia and disruptions across global 
trade routes have created fresh uncertainty around energy 
prices, logistics and availability of critical industrial inputs. 
As an import-dependent economy for crude oil and intermediate 
goods, India remains exposed to global higher energy prices, 
inflationary pressures, supply chain disruptions and commodity 
price volatility. However, diversified sourcing strategies, domestic 
manufacturing capabilities and integration with emerging 
markets are helping mitigate external risks and support industrial 
continuity.
The Government’s large-scale investments, reforms and flagship 
initiatives, such as Make in India, Production Linked Incentive (PLI) 
Schemes, have been instrumental in fostering industrial growth. 
The PLI scheme has attracted investments of approximately 
` 2.16 Lakh Crore across 14 key sectors, in line with the national 
goals like ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat’ and India’s vision of a US$ 5 
Trillion economy.
Inflation moderated significantly during the year, with the RBI 
lowering its CPI inflation forecast for FY 2025-26 to 2.1%, 
supported by favorable supply conditions and easing food 
prices. In response, the RBI reduced the repo rate cumulatively 
by 0.75% to 5.25%, supporting credit availability and investment 
activity. India’s exports are projected to approach US$ 1 Trillion in 
FY 2026-27, strengthened by trade agreements, manufacturing 
scale-up and improving export competitiveness.

(RBI), healthy capitalization, and improved balance sheets across 
Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs).
The total financing market in India, comprizing Scheduled 
Commercial Banks (SCBs) and Non-Banking Financial Companies 
(NBFCs), continued to expand during FY 2025-26. Bank credit 
growth in India remained high, reflecting healthy economic 
activity, rising private investments, and sustained consumer 
demand. As per the Ministry of Finance, credit growth of SCBs 
stood at 15.9% in FY 2025-26 compared to 10.9% in the previous 
year, while aggregate credit outstanding reached ` 212.9 Lakh 
Crore, increasing by ` 29.2 Lakh Crore over the previous year 
Stronger credit flows to NBFCs during March 2026 contributed 
significantly to the 19.0% year-on-year growth in services sector 
credit, underscoring the sector's expanding role in financial 
intermediation and credit delivery. Growth was broad-based 
across sectors, led by services, personal loans, agriculture, 
and industry. Credit to the services sector grew by 19.0%, 
supported by higher lending to NBFCs, trade, and commercial 
real estate. Industrial credit expanded by 15.0%, driven mainly 
by MSME lending, while agriculture and allied sector credit 
grew by 15.7% due to sustained rural demand and improved 
formal credit penetration. Personal loans also recorded growth 
of 16.2%, supported by housing, vehicle, and gold-backed loans. 
The continued expansion in bank credit indicates strong domestic 
demand, improved confidence among borrowers, and a stable 
banking environment supported by healthy balance sheets and 
low-stressed assets.
In FY 2025-26, India’s financial services sector continued 
to advance through greater adoption of AI-driven solutions, 
expansion of fintech services, and stronger digital public 
infrastructure. Initiatives such as the Unified Lending Interface 
(ULI) and the Account Aggregator (AA) framework enabled 
faster, more personalized credit delivery through secure data 
sharing. The sector also witnessed growth in cross-border digital 
payments and fintech integration, while Regulators increased 
focus on cybersecurity, digital resilience, and multi-currency 
payment settlement systems.
India’s digital payments ecosystem continued to expand strongly 
during FY 2025-26, supported by increasing smartphone 
penetration, merchant acceptance, and policy support from 
the Government, RBI, and NPCI. Unified Payments Interface

From a regulatory standpoint, the RBI has maintained a 
vigilant stance to ensure financial stability. The RBI, in its 
Financial Stability Report for December 2025, highlighted that 
system-level indicators relating to capital adequacy, liquidity

Non-Performing Assets (GNPA) ratios have shown steady 
improvement, reflecting a disciplined approach to asset quality 
even as credit volumes expand.

credit option in FY 2025-26, driven by increasing e-commerce 
adoption, wider digital payment integration, and borrower 
preference for flexible repayment methods. The Indian BNPL 
industry is projected to grow from US$ 30 Billion in 2025 to 
US$ 78 Billion by 2030. Concurrently, RBI has revised the 
co-lending framework, shaping the next phase of credit expansion 
by strengthening bank-NBFC partnerships, enhancing risk 
sharing and governance framework, and enabling sustainable

Outlook
The Indian financial services sector continues to witness a 
growth trajectory for the near to medium term, led by strong 
macroeconomic fundamentals, resilient policy support and 
increasing digital adoption. Credit growth is projected to remain 
steady, shaped by continued demand across renewable energy, 
MSMEs, agriculture and other emerging priority sectors. 
Strengthened asset quality and sound capital structures bolster 
resilience to potential external shocks.
India’s retail lending market is set to nearly double by FY2030 and 
now serves as the primary driver of overall loan book expansion. 
This momentum is propelled by rising disposable incomes and 
digital-first lending models that have expanded formal credit 
access to "Middle India" and young, digitally native borrowers.
Technological adaptation, such as digital platforms, AI and agentic 
AI, is anticipated to improve customer experience, operational 
efficiency and risk management abilities, allowing institutions to 
scale and manage costs effectively. Increased retail participation 
and engagement of digitally native and young customers will 
shape product innovation, with mobile-first and AI-incorporated 
channels increasing inclusion. Parallelly, to ensure more 
foreign participation and support the ability of the financial 
services for the long-term, the RBI is reviewing the current bank 
licensing and ownership norms. Capital markets are projected 
to maintain resilience, led by investor confidence, varied capital 
sources and constructive regulatory oversight. Sectoral growth 
in the future can be attributed to focused sustainable finance, 
green investment, and a rapid expansion of mutual funds. 
Emerging digital banks and wealth tech platforms are expected 
to rise, driven by increasing income levels, growing investor 
participation and enhanced financial literacy.
NBFC Sector
India’s Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) sector continued 
to play an important role in credit delivery during FY 2025-26, 
particularly in retail finance, MSME lending, vehicle finance, gold 
loans, housing finance, and rural credit. The sector supported 
financial inclusion by extending credit access to underserved 
and semi-urban markets where traditional banking penetration 
remains relatively lower. During FY 2025-26, NBFCs continued 
to strengthen their position within the retail lending ecosystem, 
supported by sustained demand across secured retail segments 
and increasing customer preference for specialized lenders. 
NBFC credit grew by around 13-15% during FY 2025-26, 
while NBFC credit grew 16.7% year-on-year in FY 2025-26. 
Retail assets remained the primary growth driver, accounting 
for nearly 57% of the sector’s credit portfolio. The growing 
contribution of NBFCs to retail lending, particularly in segments 
such as gold loans, reflects their expanding market presence, 
wider distribution reach and ability to offer faster and more 
accessible financing solutions.
The Gold Loan segment remained one of the strongest enablers 
for NBFCs, supported by rising gold prices, collateral values, and 
borrower preference for secured credit. NBFCs emerged as the 
fastest-growing lender category in gold loans, capturing nearly 
213% year-on-year growth in disbursements, outpacing public 
sector and private sector banks.This underscores their role in 
the gold loan segment through customer outreach and quick 
disbursement capabilities.
NBFCs also maintained a dominant position in the Personal Loan 
segment, particularly in smaller-ticket and digitally originated 
loans. NBFCs continued to dominate the personal loan segment 
during FY 2025-26, accounting for 91.3% of personal loan 
origination volumes and 39.8% of origination value. Their presence 
in low-ticket consumer lending continued to support credit access 
for new-to-credit and underbanked customers.
The Two-Wheeler Loan segment continued to witness NBFCs 
commanding during FY 2025-26. Owing to integrated financing 
models, streamlined underwriting practices, and outreach across 
underserved customer segments, their market position continued 
to strengthen.
NBFCs also retained leadership in the Consumer Durable Loan 
market during FY 2025-26. In FY 2025-26, NBFCs accounted 
for 85% of Consumer Durable Loan originations value and 
88% of originations volume, Their performance is attributed to

Led by resilient economic growth, MSME credit demand, 
sustained retail, and a vigilant regulatory landscape, the Indian 
NBFC sector is expected to remain buoyant. Additionally, 
data-driven underwriting, constant digitalization and fintech

scalability and operational efficiency. The stable bank-NBFC 
funding, diversification in borrowing aid funding access, 
results in strengthened liquidity and reduced refinancing

NBFC sector are likely to be boosted by calibrated regulatory 
approaches.
The evolving shift towards digitization, ESG-compliant lending, 
and retail-oriented products will shape the NBFCs business 
model of the future. NBFCs are expected to address various 
customer requirements, enhance service quality, and reinforce 
long-term customer relationships, owing to the expanded use 
of AI-driven customer insights, personalized offerings and data 
analytics. Overall, NBFCs continue to remain well-positioned by 
greater financial inclusion and long-term economic development.
Gold Loan Industry Overview
India’s gold loan market continued to expand during FY 2025-26, 
supported by rising demand for secured borrowing, increasing 
gold prices, and stronger participation from organized lenders. 
Gold-backed financing remained a preferred credit option for 
individuals, small businesses, traders, and rural households due 
to faster loan processing, lower documentation requirements, 
and immediate liquidity availability. The Indian gold loan is 
emerging as the fastest-growing segment within retail credit as 
the outstanding gold loans increased from approximately ` 12.4 
Lakh Crore in March 2025 to ` 18.6 Lakh Crore in March 2026, 
reflecting 50.4% year-on-year growth, supported by rising gold 
prices, higher ticket sizes and strong demand for secured credit. 
industry is benefiting from increasing demand for accessible 
credit and continued strength in gold prices.

Micro Finance Industry (MFI)
The Micro Finance Industry in India remains a key contributor to 
advancing financial services, expanding credit and allied financial 
services in underserved communities. Over time, the sector 
has witnessed significant transformation, driven by increasing 
technology adoption to enhance outreach, a structured 
regulatory framework and improving customer experience. 
Particularly, NBFC-MFIs play an integral role in the formal 
financial landscape, enhancing inclusive growth and access to 
finance for economically vulnerable citizens.
Owing to the government-led measures, such as Pradhan 
Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY), Pradhan Mantri MUDRA 
Yojana (PMMY), Atal Pension Yojana (APY), and similar initiatives, 
the foundation of the sector is strengthened. These programs 
are aimed at widening access to banking, household credits, 
insurance, and pensions outside the formal financial structures. 
In these contexts, MFIs function as effective last-mile delivery 
sources, connecting informal economic participants and 
regulated financial institutions. With its focused lending to 
self-employed individuals, women and small entrepreneurs, the 
industry contributes to livelihood creation, social empowerment, 
and income generation, strengthening its relevance in India’s 
inclusive development objectives.

India’s microfinance industry witnessed a phase of consolidation 
during FY 2025-26 after a period of rapid expansion in previous 
years. The sector remained focused on maintaining portfolio 
quality, improving underwriting standards, and strengthening 
borrower discipline amid liquidity constraints and stress 
in unsecured lending segments. Despite moderation in 
disbursements, Microfinance Institutions (MFIs) continued to play 
an important role in providing financial access to low-income 
households, women borrowers, and rural entrepreneurs across 
the country.
According to the Microfinance Industry Network (MFIN) Report 
for Q3 FY 2025-26, microfinance operations were spread across 
36 states and union territories covering over 714 districts as of 
December 31, 2025. The overall microfinance portfolio stood at 
approximately ` 3.15 Lakh Crore, reflecting moderation in portfolio 
growth due to cautious lending practices and slower wholesale 
funding availability to NBFC-MFIs. NBFC-MFIs remained the 
largest category of lenders with a 42.1% share of the industry 
portfolio, followed by banks and small finance banks.
The sector witnessed lower disbursement volumes during 
the first half of FY 2025-26 due to tighter underwriting norms

Automobile Industry
India’s automobile industry recorded its highest-ever annual sales 
across all major vehicle categories during FY 2025-26, supported 
by strong consumer demand, favorable policy measures, lower 
financing costs, and improving economic activity. According to 
the latest data released by the Society of Indian Automobile 
Manufacturers, the industry witnessed broad-based growth 
across passenger vehicles, commercial vehicles, two-wheelers, 
and three-wheelers.
Passenger vehicle sales reached a record 4.64 Million during 
FY 2025-26, registering growth of 7.9% over the previous year. 
The segment benefited from improved affordability following 
GST reforms, personal income tax relief measures, and multiple 
repo rate cuts by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which reduced 
financing costs for consumers. Electric passenger vehicle 
registrations also increased significantly during the year, 
contributing to overall segment growth. Passenger vehicle 
exports reached an all-time high of approximately 0.91 Million 
supported by steady demand from the Middle East, Africa, and 
Latin America.
The two-wheeler segment recorded its highest-ever annual 
sales of 21.71 Million in FY 2025-26, reflecting growth of 10.7% 
over the previous year and surpassing the earlier peak achieved 
in FY 2018-19. Growth was driven by stronger urban demand, 
improved financing availability, and increasing adoption of 
electric two-wheelers. Exports of two-wheelers also reached a 
record 5.18 Million during the year, registering growth of 23.4%, 
supported by wider global acceptance of Indian brands and 
competitive pricing.
The commercial vehicle segment posted its highest-ever sales 
of 1.08 Million during FY 2025-26, registering growth of 12.6% 
compared to FY 2024-25. Increased infrastructure activity, 
higher capital expenditure, stronger fleet replacement demand, 
and improved logistics movement supported segment growth. 
Lower borrowing costs following repo rate reductions also 
encouraged vehicle purchases by transport operators and fleet 
owners. Commercial vehicle exports increased by 17.4% during 
the year to around .10 Million units.
Three-wheeler sales also reached a record level of 0.84 Million 
in FY 2025-26, growing by 12.8% year-on-year. Demand was 
supported by increasing urban mobility requirements, growth 
in e-commerce logistics, and rising penetration of electric 
autorickshaws. Expansion of permit issuance for internal 
combustion engine (ICE) three-wheelers in select states also 
contributed positively to industry growth.
Overall automobile production in India stood at 2.83 Million.units 
during FY 2025-26, reflecting strong manufacturing activity 
and sustained domestic demand. The industry also benefited 
from improving macroeconomic conditions, rising consumer 
confidence, and increasing adoption of electric mobility solutions.
The increasing availability of vehicle financing remained an 
important growth driver, supporting the industry's expansion. 
With softer interest rates, enhanced loan-to-value norms, 
and wider outreach of NBFCs across rural and semi-urban 
geographies, affordability has improved. Additionally, 
enhancements in borrower credit profiles facilitated the 
participation of the first-time buyer group, contributing to stable 
sectoral growth.

growth. Competitive lending rates, increased credit access and 
a wide range of financing products support the steady demand 
across commercial, passenger and two-wheeler segments. 
To sustain vehicle sales, financing-led affordability plays a 
crucial role, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas, followed 
by formal credit expansion. Flexibility in repayment structures 
and loan product customization has further increased vehicle 
ownership, addressing broader mobility requirements across 
various income groups.

growth during FY 2025-26. The outstanding auto loan portfolio 
increased from ` 8.2 Lakh Crore as of March 2025 to ` 9.3 Lakh 
Crore as of March 2026, registering a year-on-year growth of 
13.9%. The number of active auto loans also increased from 
158.9 Lakhs to 171.6 Lakhs during the same period, reflecting 
sustained vehicle demand and continued credit penetration 
across customer segments.

Housing Finance Industry
The housing finance sector in India continued to witness stable 
growth during FY 2025-26, supported by urbanization, rising 
household income, favorable demographics, and continued 
policy support for affordable housing. The sector remains 
an important contributor to residential demand, financial 
inclusion, and infrastructure development across urban and 
semi-urban markets.
The total housing loan portfolio across banks, Non-Banking 
Financial Companies (NBFCs), and Housing Finance Companies 
(HFCs) reached approximately ` 40.8 Lakh Crore in 2025, 
registering around 10% year-on-year growth. Housing Finance 
Companies (HFCs) recorded nearly 12% credit growth during 
FY 2025-26, while their Assets Under Management (AUM) 
increased to approximately ` 9.8 Lakh Crore, reflecting nearly 
15% year-on-year growth. The sector continued to benefit from 
sustained demand across salaried, self-employed, and affordable 
housing borrower segments.
Housing finance demand also expanded in semi-urban and 
emerging markets due to wider lender presence, improved digital 
underwriting systems, and increasing accessibility of formal 
credit. Housing loans as a percentage of GDP increased from 
around 8% in FY 2014-15 to approximately 11% in FY 2024-25, 
reflecting deeper mortgage penetration within the economy. 
India’s housing finance market is estimated at approximately 
US$ 430.74 Billion in 2026 and is projected to reach nearly 
US$ 809.07 Billion by 2031, growing at a CAGR of 13.44%.
The interest rate environment during FY 2025-26 remained 
relatively supportive for housing demand. The Reserve Bank 
of India (RBI) maintained a moderately accommodative stance, 
with the repo rate easing to around 5.25% during FY 2025-26. 
Stable borrowing costs supported affordability and sustained 
demand for housing loans across borrower categories. 
However, lenders remained cautious in credit underwriting amid 
evolving macroeconomic conditions and moderation in overall 
retail credit growth.
The industry continued to remain diversified and competitive, 
with Public Sector Banks retaining a dominant position in housing 
credit. Private sector banks strengthened their market presence 
through digital capabilities and faster loan processing, while 
HFCs focused on affordable housing, self-employed borrowers, 
and underserved customer segments. Total disbursements of 
HFC’s grew 19.5% year-on-year, highlighting their continued role 
in last-mile credit delivery.
Affordable housing continued to remain a key growth segment 
during the year. . Affordable Housing Finance Companies (AHFCs) 
also recorded strong growth, with AUM increasing nearly 
19% year-on-year to approximately ` 1,58,449 Crores during 
FY 2025-26. Demand remained strong among informal income 
borrowers and first-time homebuyers.
The sector’s financial profile remained stable during the 
year, supported by healthy capitalization levels, diversified 
funding sources, and prudent underwriting practices. 
Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPA) for HFCs remained stable 
at around 1.7%, indicating healthy portfolio quality despite 
broader stress in unsecured retail lending segments. As the 
sector evolves, AUM growth is anticipated to normalize to healthy 
and sustainable levels of around 20% by FY 2026-27.

was supported by increasing awareness, regulatory support 
under the ‘Insurance for All by 2047’ initiative and rising private 
sector participation. The retail segment accounted for nearly 65% 
of the market in 2025 and is expected to grow at a CAGR of 12.4% 
through 2031.
The life insurance industry witnessed a strong recovery 
during FY 2025-26, with new business premiums increasing 
by 15.7% year-on-year to ` 4.60 Lakh Crore, compared with a 
growth of 5.1% in FY 2024-25. Private insurers outpaced the 
industry growth, recording a 16.7% increase in new business 
premiums, while LIC reported a growth of 14.9%. The recovery 
was supported by improved traction in both individual and 
group businesses, normalization of business volumes following 
regulatory changes and increased demand for protection and 
savings products. The sustained growth momentum, coupled with 
expanding distribution channels and digital initiatives, reinforces 
the long-term growth potential of the life insurance sector.India 
currently ranks as the fifth-largest life insurance market among 
emerging economies and is expected to become the sixth-largest 
insurance market globally within the next decade.
The industry also witnessed increasing preference for 
protection-oriented and non-participating (non-par) products 
due to higher profitability, capital efficiency, and guaranteed 
return structures. Unit Linked Insurance Plans (ULIPs) continued 
to record strong demand as tax-efficient, market-linked 
investment products combined with life insurance protection. 
Growth in the group insurance and credit life segment remained 
linked to expanding retail lending, with India’s retail loan portfolio 
increasing to ` 162.7 Lakh Crore, reflecting 18.1% year-on-year 
growth and nearly 690 Million active loan accounts.
Annuity and pension products continued to gain importance due 
to rising longevity and increasing retirement planning awareness. 
India’s pension ecosystem also expanded significantly, with 
National Pension System (NPS) subscribers reaching 211.7 Lakhs 
and assets under management rising to approximately ` 16.1 
Lakh Crore. Despite increasing financialization, pension assets 
remain relatively low at around 14% of GDP, creating long-term 
growth opportunities for retirement-focused insurance products.
Regulatory reforms continued to support industry development 
during the year. The Insurance Regulatory and Development 
Authority of India (IRDAI) continued to advance its ‘Insurance 
for All by 2047’ initiative to improve insurance penetration 
and accessibility. IRDAI also proposed mandatory adoption 
of Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) from April 1, 2026, to 
improve transparency and align the sector with global reporting 
practices. The transition towards Risk-Based Capital (RBC) norms 
is expected to strengthen underwriting discipline and capital 
efficiency. Additionally, IRDAI is working on reforms relating to 
commission structures and the proposed ‘Bima Sugam’ digital 
marketplace to improve customer accessibility, transparency, 
and digital insurance distribution
(Source: Mordor intelligence, IBEF, CRIF, PIB, , PIB, , IRDAI, Persistence 
market research, IRDAI, IBEF, Careratings)
Outlook
The medium-to-long term outlook for the Insurance industry 
in India remains positive, augmented by multiple structural 
drivers such as increasing disposable income, rising protection 
awareness and constant digital integration. The industry offers 
substantial opportunities for growth, is driven by broader market 
access of Tier II and Tier III cities, a young workforce, and an 
evolving preference of customers towards retirement-focused 
and protection-oriented solutions.
In the regulatory landscape, initiatives of the Insurance 
Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) include 
streamlining product approval, increasing foreign direct 
investment limits up to 100% and sustaining emphasis on 
financial inclusion, all of which provide a supportive operating 
environment for insurers. Advancements in digital technologies, 
including artificial intelligence, end-to-end digital onboarding and 
data analytics, further reinforce underwriting capabilities, fraud 
management and customer experience. Similarly, insurers are 
diversifying product offerings to address the changing needs 
of women, senior citizens and gig economy participants and 
progressively integrating Environment, Social and Governance 
(ESG) considerations into business strategies. With the insurers 
evolving to become financial solution partners comprehensively, 
the industry is projected to play a critical role in long-term savings, 
capital formation and socio-economic development in India.

Business Review
Manappuram Finance Limited, with its focused yet diversified 
business model, operates primarily in gold-backed lending 
while steadily expanding its presence across complementary 
financial services, including microfinance, affordable housing 
finance, vehicle and equipment finance, MSME lending and allied 
businesses. Gold loans continue to remain the cornerstone of 
the Company’s operations, supported by a scalable, low-ticket 
and short-tenure lending model that leverages India’s significant 
household gold holdings. During FY 2025-26, the Company’s 
consolidated gold loan AUM stood at ` 50,953 Crores, 
registering a strong year-on-year growth of 99.1%, reaffirming 
the segment’s role as the primary growth driver of the business.
By providing quick and secured credit against pledged gold 
jewelry, the Company continues to address borrowers’ 
short-term liquidity requirements, particularly in rural and 
semi-urban regions with relatively lower penetration of formal 
banking services. The inherent strengths of the gold loan 
business, including shorter loan maturities, high portfolio churn 
and secured collateral-backed lending, continue to support risk 
management and balance sheet resilience. The Company has 
also strengthened its product framework in line with revised 
regulatory guidelines by introducing consumption loans 
and income-generating loans within defined LTV and tenure 
guardrails, enabling more structured customer segmentation 
and improved underwriting standards.
The Company along with its subsidiaries operates through an 
extensive branch network of over 5,000 branches across the 
country with a consolidated employee base of more than 42,000 
employees, enabling penetration into underbanked geographies. 
Speed and convenience remain central to the Company’s 
operating model. Standardized appraisal mechanisms, 
real-time credit evaluation and technology-enabled processes 
facilitate faster loan disbursement and enhanced customer 
servicing. Branch-level operational flexibility, exercised within 
clearly-defined risk management and governance frameworks, 
further enhances responsiveness and execution efficiency.
Over the years, the Company has built a trusted brand franchise 
in the gold loan industry, strengthened by its long-standing 
customer relationships and operational rigor in managing 
appraisal, custodial and valuation risks. Continued investments in 
digital capabilities are further enhancing customer engagement 
and operational productivity. The Company’s Online Gold Loan 
(OGL) platform, one of the earliest digital gold loan solutions 
introduced by an NBFC in India, enables eligible borrowers to avail, 
renew and manage gold loans digitally through seamless and 
paperless processes. Supported by integrated digital KYC, instant 
approvals, repayment tracking and re-pledge functionalities, 
the Company continues to strengthen customer convenience, 
accessibility and turnaround efficiency. Backed by its operational 
capabilities, diversified lending franchise and technology-led 
ecosystem, the Company remains well-positioned to achieve 
growth in the evolving digital financial services landscape.
Business Performance in FY 2025-26
During FY 2025-26, Manappuram Finance Limited delivered 
a resilient operational performance despite a challenging 
macroeconomic environment and stress in select unsecured 
lending segments. The Company continued to strengthen its 
position in secured lending, particularly in the gold loan business, 
while adopting a calibrated and risk-conscious approach across 
microfinance, vehicle finance, MSME lending and housing finance 
operations. Supported by strong customer demand, favorable 
gold prices and disciplined underwriting practices, the Company 
maintained business momentum and balance sheet strength 
during the year.
The Company’s consolidated Assets Under Management (AUM) 
increased by 48.3% YoY to ` 63,798 Crores in FY 2025-26 from 
` 43,034 Crores in FY 2024-25, primarily led by expansion in the 
gold loan portfolio. Consolidated revenue from operations stood 
at ` 9,509 Crores during the year, while Profit After Tax (PAT) 
stood at ` 993 Crores. The Company maintained a strong capital 
position with a Standalone Capital Adequacy Ratio (CRAR) of 
21.3%, supported by diversified borrowing sources and prudent 
liquidity management.
Gold loans remained the primary growth engine of the Company 
during FY 2025-26. Consolidated gold loan AUM rose sharply 
by 99.1% YoY to ` 50,953 Crores, accounting for nearly 80% of 
the consolidated AUM compared with 59% in the previous year. 
The strong growth was supported by rising gold prices, increased 
economic activity, improving rural demand and growing customer 
preference for secured credit products. The Company added 
approximately 3.16 Lakh new customers during Q4 FY 2025-26 
alone, taking the consolidated outstanding customer base to 
around 27.11 Lakh customers. Gold holdings under management 
increased to approximately 63 tons as of March 31, 2026.
During the year, the Company further strengthened its gold loan 
product framework in line with revised regulatory guidelines 
governing lending against gold collateral. The Company 
introduced new product categories comprizing consumption 
loans and income-generating loans, enabling it to cater more 
effectively to household financing requirements, livelihood and 
small business funding. These products were launched with 
defined guardrails relating to loan-to-value (LTV) ratios, customer 
eligibility and tenure structures, improving underwriting discipline 
and customer segmentation. The revised framework also 
enhanced customer due diligence practices and strengthened 
delinquency management.
The Company continued to invest significantly in digital 
capabilities and process innovation during FY 2025-26. 
The Company’s Online Gold Loan (OGL) platform witnessed 
strong adoption, with online gold loans accounting for 
approximately 92% of the total gold loan portfolio by the end 
of Q4 FY 2025-26. Through integrated digital KYC processes, 
instant approvals, online repayment systems and re-pledge 
functionalities, the Company enhanced customer convenience,

with consolidated cash and cash equivalents of ` 6,149 Crores 
as of March 31, 2026.
With continued emphasis on secured lending, digital 
transformation, operational efficiency and prudent risk 
management, the Company remains well positioned to capitalize 
on long-term opportunities in the financial services sector while 
maintaining sustainable and balanced growth across business 
verticals.

Risk Management
In an evolving financial services landscape, effective risk 
management remains fundamental, supporting long-term 
stability and growth of Financial Institutions. The Company, a 
well-established Non-Banking Financial Company in India, 
operates in a tightly regulated and competitive landscape, 
exposing it to various operational, financial and external risks. 
The proactive risk management approach of the Company 
centers on identifying potential risk exposures, analyzing 
their impact, defining acceptable risk and implementing 
appropriate mitigating strategies. This framework is supported 
by strong governance mechanisms, ongoing monitoring and 
comprehensive policies, which enable the Company to manage 
risk across functional areas. By embedding risk considerations 
into strategic decision-making and everyday operational 
execution, the Company strengthens its business resilience while 
protecting stakeholder interests.
Credit Risk: Credit risk arises from the failure of borrowers to 
fulfill their repayment obligations, resulting in financial losses. 
In the Company, this risk is intrinsic to its lending processes, 
particularly in unsecured portfolios such as Microfinance and 
MSME financing.
The Company manages credit risk through a product-specific 
underwriting framework, supported by processes, which include 
customer profiling, financial analysis, cash flow, credit history 
evaluation and systematic risk classification. Considering secured 
products, the current monitoring of collateral adequacy and 
liquidity parameters is reviewed to ensure sufficient risk 
coverage. Portfolio diversification strategies are integrated to

minimize concentration risks. Additionally, technology-enabled 
loan processing and a centralized credit decision framework 
strengthen governance by mitigating subjectivity and ensuring 
consistent policy adherence. Early warning mechanisms timely 
detect stress indicators, instigating proactive interventions by 
restructuring and focused recovery methods.
Technology Risk: Technology risk arises from the possibility 
of losses due to failures, disruptions and weaknesses 
in the Company’s information technology environment. 
This encompasses risks, including system downtime, cyber 
threats, data compromise, technology obsolescence, and 
application malfunctions. With the increasing digital platforms 
across lending, servicing and consumer engagement, it is crucial 
to scale technology systems to ensure uninterrupted operations 
and customer experience.
To reduce these risks, the Company continues to maintain a 
scalable technology infrastructure, designed to reinforce current 
operations and future growth. IT oversight is monitored through 
a focused governance framework, responsible for application 
security, timely technology enhancement, system reliability and 
vendor oversight. Cyber security remains a core priority in the 
Company that includes network firewall, encryption standard 
and intrusion detection. Owing to its current vulnerability 
assessments, penetration testing and cyber threats surveillance, 
the Company proactively identifies and mitigates potential 
exposures.
The Company also establishes comprehensive disaster recovery 
and business continuity frameworks such as automated data 
backups, alternate processing facilities and periodic simulation 
exercises to validate preparedness. Continuous employee 
awareness of information security reinforces internal controls. 
In parallel, the Company continuously monitors technology 
advancements and evolving cybersecurity threats to align its IT 
strategy with industry-based practices.
Interest Rate Risk: Interest rate risk arises from the potential 
variations in prevailing market interest rates, impacting the 
financial position, balance sheet volumes and earnings of the 
Company. Fluctuating rates can impact interest income and 
expense, influence the carrying value of assets and liabilities and 
affect overall profitability across different interest rate cycles.
The Company addresses this risk through a comprehensive 
Asset-Liability Management (ALM) framework, focused on 
aligning asset and liability maturities and repricing characteristics 
to limit timing and rate mismatches. The ALM committee is 
responsible for periodically reviewing interest rate scenarios, 
market developments, and calibrating lending strategies 
accordingly.
Additionally, the Company selectively employs hedging 
instruments such as interest rate swaps where appropriate, 
to reduce exposure to rate volatility. Periodic stress testing 
and sensitivity analysis are conducted to gauge the impact of 
volatility of the interest rates allowing the Company to formulate 
appropriate risk mitigation processes and contingency measures.
Operational Risk: Operational risks arise due to potential 
breakdowns in internal processes, personnel, systems or external 
factors, adversely affecting business operations. Key sources of 
such risk include system outages, fraudulent activities, human 
error or unforeseen events, caused by external activities.
The Company addresses these risks by leveraging 
technology-driven solutions, simplifying workflows and 
minimizing manual interventions. A dedicated Internal Audit 
team periodically reviews operational practices to understand 
adherence to internal controls while recommending remedial 
measures, if required. With regular employee trainings focused 
on operational discipline, fraud risk awareness, and service 
delivery standards, the Company continues to strengthen its 
operational resilience.
Liquidity Risk: The Company's possibility to face liquidity risk 
emerges from its difficulties in meeting financial obligations on 
time, affecting its cost structure. Such risk may emerge from 
asset-liability maturity mismatches and unexpected funding 
requirements or disrupted funding markets.
Maintaining a well-diversified funding mix, drawing resources 
from banks, debt markets and institutional investors, leads the 
Company to manage this risk. The Treasury team plays a crucial 
role in forecasting funding requirements while undertaking 
forward-looking assessments, ensuring the timely availability 
of liquidity in business operations.
The Company further implements a structured liquidity risk 
model, encompassing the maintenance of sufficient liquidity 
buffers, regular monitoring of cash flows and well-defined 
contingency funding arrangements. The Asset-Liability 
Committee is responsible for reviewing key liquidity metrics, 
providing further guidance on funding and investment actions 
to maintain economic stability.
Regulatory and Compliance Risk: Regulatory and compliance 
risk arises from the possibility of business restrictions, 
disruptions or sanctions, resulting from non-compliance 
with regulatory directives, industry standards and prevailing 
laws. Given the evolving regulatory expectations governing 
Non-Banking Financial Companies, the Company is required 
to align its operations with evolving legal, supervisory, and 
governance requirements.
The Company puts forth a comprehensive compliance and 
governance framework, overseen by a dedicated Compliance 
team to manage this risk. Policies, control mechanisms and 
procedures are regularly improved to embed regulatory 
changes. The Company's automated compliance tool, defined 
approval process, and real-time monitoring systems ensure 
timely identification and mitigation of compliance risk.
Regulatory compliance oversight is implemented by the 
Company’s Board of Directors and its Committees, led by regular 
reviews conducted by Independent Auditors. Ongoing training 
and awareness programs are conducted to strengthen 
compliance awareness and ethical conduct in the company.

Reputational Risk: Reputational risk refers to the potential 
erosion of stakeholder trust, arising from actual or perceived 
shortcomings in conduct, consumer experience, and governance. 
Damage to reputation may affect consumer confidence, involve 
regulatory attention, affecting the Company's funding profile.
The Company’s adherence to the well-defined code of conduct, 
its clearly articulated customer service practices, and transparent 
disclosures effectively mitigate this risk. To address customer 
complaints, formal grievance redressal channels are embedded 
into the Company as a structured feedback process, leading to 
constant service delivery improvement. With its defined crisis 
management and communication protocols, the Company 
addresses reputational concerns promptly. The public relations, 
communication team, and senior leadership work collaboratively 
to manage media interactions, ensuring clear and consistent 
stakeholder engagement.
Competition Risk: Competition risk arises when the Company is 
unable to execute competitive strategies effectively or respond 
promptly to evolving market trends. Entering new markets or 
launching additional financial products without significant 
preparedness may lead the Company to witness unforeseen 
operational or strategic challenges.
The Company adopts disciplined strategy planning, reinforced 
by detailed market analysis, scenario-based assessment and 
risk-reward evaluation. The major strategic initiatives undergo 
Senior Management's review and are subject to the Board's 
approval, maintaining consistency with the Company’s long-term 
objectives and risk tolerance.
Key performance metrics and milestone-based monitoring 
frameworks track the Company’s execution process, supporting 
early identification of deviations and corrective measures. 
With the integration of periodic risk reviews into its planning 
process, the Company recalibrates its strategies in response to 
changes in the macroeconomic environment.
Asset or Security Risk: Asset or security risk occurs when the 
value of collateral potentially erodes, impairing the Company’s 
recoverability of outstanding loans. This risk is mostly pronounced 
in the Company’s secured lending products, including gold loans 
or other asset-backed financing.
The Company follows prudent loan-to-value norms, undertaking 
regular reviews of collateral valuations to reduce its exposure. 
In gold loan portfolios, the purity, quality, and prevailing 
market value of the pledged gold are assessed at the time of 
disbursement while monitoring over the loan tenure to ensure 
sufficient collateral coverage.
Additionally, the Company employs stress-testing frameworks 
to analyze the sensitivity of collateral values to unfavorable 
market conditions. Based on these assessments, timely collective 
actions, including revising loan conditions for seeking incremental 
collateral, are implemented to limit potential losses.
Human Capital Risk: Human capital risk reflects potential 
misalignment between the Company’s people management 
frameworks and its operation and strategic requirements. 
This includes risks related to talent acquisition, employee 
retention, workforce motivation, and leadership continuity.
Succession planning remains the core element in the people 
strategy of the Company, reinforcing its continuity in key 
managerial and operational roles. The Company integrates 
a performance evaluation framework, aligning individual 
responsibilities with organizational priorities, enabling proactive 
identification and resolution of performance gaps.
Economic Risk: Economic risk emerges from changes in 
macroeconomic variables, including inflation, economic growth, 
labor market conditions and interest rates, affecting the 
Company's operating environment and profitability.
The Company continuously monitors key economic indicators, 
incorporating economic outlooks into its planning and risk 
management methods. Scenario-based evaluations and stress 
testing are conducted to evaluate the potential effects of 
unfavorable cycles on the Company's financial strength.
Exposure is reduced through portfolio diversification across 
industries and geographies, limiting vulnerability to localized 
economic slowdowns. Additionally, the Company maintains 
adequate capital buffers and liquidity reserves to withstand 
economic volatility.

Internal Control
The Company has implemented a comprehensive internal 
control system to promote operational effectiveness, ensure 
adherence to regulatory requirements and manage risk across 
its financial services activities. The control framework covers 
critical functions, including credit appraisal, loan disbursements, 
collection, finance, compliance, and information technology. 
With its well-defined organizational structure, led by clearly 
articulated roles, system-driven controls and documented 
policies, the Company reinforces its accountability and 
transparency.
Internal controls are integrated into core business processes 
through maker-checker mechanisms, approval hierarchies, 
and automated validations to reduce human errors and 
prevent unauthorized activities. The Internal Audit functions 
independently and reports directly to the Board’s Audit 
Committee. The Committee is responsible for periodic risk-focused 
audits across functional units to analyze controlled adequacy, 
identify process gaps and puts fourth corrective measures. 
Corrective actions are monitored to ensure timely closure.
The Company places strong emphasis on internal controls 
over financial reporting to ensure the accuracy and reliability of 
financial disclosures. Digital tools and management dashboards 
facilitate constant monitoring of important operational indicators 
and exceptions. Periodic training programs are conducted to 
familiarize employees with control processes and compliance 
obligations to foster a culture of responsibility. As the business 
scales and integrates digital solutions, the internal control 
framework is continuously reinforced to address emerging 
risks. Overall, the Company’s internal control system is proactive, 
effective and adequate and integral to sustaining operational 
discipline and stakeholder confidence.

R Customer over-indebtedness is a material risk in the financial 
services sector, particularly for Non-Banking Financial 
Companies (NBFCs) serving low- and middle-income segments. 
Excessive borrowing without adequate repayment capacity can 
lead to financial distress for customers, higher default rates for 
lenders, and reputational or regulatory consequences for the 
institution. Manappuram Finance Limited proactively addresses 
this risk by implementing rigorous credit assessments across its 
non-gold lending verticals. This includes evaluating household 
income, existing liabilities, and repayment capacity before loan 
disbursement. By doing so, the Company mitigates the risk of 
customer over-indebtedness, reduces dependency on informal 
credit channels, and upholds responsible lending practices. This 
approach not only protects customer financial well-being but 
also safeguards the Company’s asset quality and long-term 
sustainability.
Manappuram Finance Limited adopts a multi-layered approach 
to mitigate the risk of customer over indebtedness, with a 
strong focus on responsible lending and financial inclusion. The 
Company enforces stringent loan eligibility criteria, taking into 
account the applicant’s income, existing debt obligations, and 
overall creditworthiness to ensure that loan disbursements are 
well within the borrower’s repayment capacity. Comprehensive 
borrower assessments are conducted to align loan amounts 
with actual financial stability, thereby reducing the likelihood of 
debt distress. In addition, robust monitoring systems are in place 
to track repayment behaviour and identify early warning signals 
of potential over-indebtedness, enabling timely intervention. 
To further support financial resilience among its customers, 
the Company has implemented targeted financial literacy 
programmes. These initiatives aim to educate borrowers on 
budgeting, debt management, and the importance of maintaining 
healthy financial habits, thereby empowering them to make 
informed borrowing decisions.

treatment facilities as part of its resource efficiency efforts. Waste management practices

secure e-waste disposal through authorised recyclers following data-wiping protocols, and

opportunities for team-building, social engagement, and professional development.

CSR initiatives spanning diagnostic and ambulance services (MaCare Diagnostics and

yoga facilities, and the Mahima swimming pool), education and skill development support

At Manappuram Finance Limited, the Company’s commitment to responsible growth is 
guided by a deep understanding of the environmental, social, and governance (ESG) issues 
that affect its stakeholders. As part of its Business Responsibility and Sustainability approach, 
the Company has identified and prioritised material topics that represent both risks and 
opportunities to long-term value creation.
Employee well-being remains a key opportunity area. The Company continues to invest in its 
workforce through comprehensive benefits, including health and group insurance, maternity 
benefits, leave entitlements, employee welfare schemes, team-building programmes, and 
professional development initiatives. Its sustained focus on diversity and inclusion, financial 
inclusion, and responsible financing supports equitable access and underpins a resilient 
business model.
Measurable progress has been made towards the Company’s sustainability goals during FY 
2025-26. A 14.9% reduction in energy intensity per unit of revenue and a 17.11% reduction 
in combined Scope 1 and Scope 2 emission intensity per rupee of turnover were achieved, 
demonstrating the Company’s commitment to operational efficiency and decarbonisation.
Investments in solar energy (113 MWh consumed during the year), the expansion of the 
electric vehicle fleet (124,143 km travelled, resulting in estimated emissions savings of 
14,590 kgCO₂e), and enhancements to sewage treatment infrastructure further advance the 
Company’s clean technology adoption and low-carbon transition objectives.
The Company acknowledges significant ESG-related risks that necessitate active monitoring 
and mitigation. Key risk areas include customer support and satisfaction, over-indebtedness, 
climate change, corporate governance, business ethics, regulatory compliance, and fraud risk 
management. Addressing these areas is fundamental to maintaining stakeholder trust and 
ensuring long-term operational stability.
The Company’s community impact reflects its core values. Through CSR initiatives 
encompassing MaCare Diagnostics, ambulance services, sports and wellness infrastructure, 
school and skill-building support, and professional education coaching through MaCampus 
and MaAcademy, the Company positively impacted 303,982 individuals during the reporting 
period, of whom 99% belonged to vulnerable or marginalised communities.
The Company recognises that while substantial progress has been achieved, significant 
opportunities remain. Efforts are underway to formalise specific, measurable ESG targets and 
strengthen risk-response mechanisms. The Company’s forward-looking strategy will further 
integrate ESG considerations across business operations, reinforcing resilience and enabling 
responsible value creation for all stakeholders.

4. Does the entity have an anti-corruption or anti-bribery policy? If yes, provide details in brief and if available, provide a web-link 
to the policy.
 Yes. Manappuram Finance Limited has adopted a comprehensive anti-corruption and anti-bribery policy framework designed to 
promote ethical conduct and prevent misconduct at all levels of the organisation. The key policies constituting this framework 
are as follows:
 1. Whistle Blower Policy and Vigil Mechanism: This policy provides all stakeholders — including employees, directors, 
vendors, and customers — with a secure channel to raise genuine concerns regarding illegal or unethical practices, 
including bribery, fraud, corruption, or the unauthorised disclosure of Unpublished Price-Sensitive Information (UPSI). 
The policy provides direct access to the Chairman of the Audit Committee, ensures strict confidentiality, and guarantees 
protection against retaliation or victimisation for disclosures made in good faith.
 2. Code of Conduct to Regulate, Monitor, and Report Trading by Designated Persons in Securities: Framed in accordance 
with Regulation 9(1) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, this code safeguards against insider 
trading by ensuring the confidentiality of Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) and prohibiting designated 
persons and their immediate relatives from trading in the Company’s securities while in possession of UPSI.
 3. Code of Practices and Procedures for Fair Disclosure of UPSI: Framed in accordance with Regulation 8(1) of the SEBI 
(Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, this code mandates the fair and non-selective dissemination of UPSI, 
reinforcing transparency and integrity in the Company’s public disclosures.
 4. Fair Practice Code (FPC): Issued pursuant to the Reserve Bank of India’s guidelines for Master Direction - Reserve Bank 
of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, November 28 th 2025, this code 
establishes standards for fair and ethical conduct in lending, recovery, and customer service delivery.
 Collectively, these policies reinforce the Company’s internal governance framework, uphold ethical conduct across all business 
activities, and deter corruption and bribery. The full text of all policy documents is available on the Company’s official website: 
https://www.manappuram.com/policies-codes

details of the same.
 Yes. Manappuram Finance Limited has established well-defined processes to prevent and manage conflicts of interest involving 
members of its Board of Directors. The key frameworks in place are as follows:
  Policy on Related Party Transactions: The Company has implemented a Policy on Related Party Transactions 
to mitigate potential conflicts arising from dealings with related parties, including Board members. The policy 
establishes guidelines and procedures for identifying, evaluating, and managing such transactions, ensuring 
they are conducted at arm’s length and in the best interests of the Company and its stakeholders.
  Code of Conduct to Regulate, Monitor, and Report Trading by Designated Persons in Securities: Framed 
in accordance with Regulation 9(1) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, this code 
safeguards against insider trading by regulating, monitoring, and reporting securities trading by designated 
persons. It prohibits designated persons and their immediate relatives from trading in the Company’s securities 
while in possession of Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI), thereby upholding securities laws and 
protecting the Company’s integrity.
  Code of Practices and Procedures for Fair Disclosure of Unpublished Price Sensitive Information: Framed 
in accordance with Regulation 8(1) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, this code 
mandates the equitable and non-selective dissemination of UPSI, establishing clear principles, procedures, 
and practices for its uniform and fair disclosure by the Company.
  Fair Practice Code (FPC): Issued pursuant to the Reserve Bank of India’s guidelines for Non-Banking Financial 
Companies and updated in compliance with the Master Direction - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking 
Financial Companies - Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, November 28th 2025, this code establishes 
ethical standards for fair and responsible lending, recovery, and customer service practices.

5. Describe the internal mechanisms in place to redress grievances related to human rights issues.
 Manappuram Finance Limited has established structured internal mechanisms to redress grievances relating to human rights 
and to ensure a fair, respectful, and inclusive working environment. The key frameworks in place are as follows:
 Prevention of Sexual Harassment (POSH): The Company has constituted Internal Complaints Committees (ICCs) at its Registered 
Office and regional locations in accordance with the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition 
and Redressal) Act, 2013. Employees may submit complaints in writing or through a dedicated email channel. All complaints 
are handled with strict confidentiality, investigated impartially, and resolved in accordance with the provisions of the Act. 
Recommendations of the ICC are duly implemented, and an appeal mechanism is available as prescribed under the law.
 Employee Grievance Redressal: The Company has a formal Employee Grievance Redressal Policy that enables employees to 
raise workplace concerns through a structured escalation process. Employees are encouraged to first approach their reporting 
manager; unresolved matters may be escalated to the HR Grievance Officer through the internal grievance portal. All grievances 
are reviewed, investigated, and resolved within defined timelines, with further escalation to senior management where warranted.
 Together, these mechanisms reflect the Company's commitment to upholding human rights, ensuring equal opportunity and 
dignity in the workplace, and providing all employees with access to a transparent and effective grievance redressal process.

1. Describe the mechanisms in place to receive and respond to consumer complaints and feedback.
 Manappuram Finance Limited fosters a customer-centric culture with the objective of maintaining stakeholder trust and 
satisfaction. The Company takes all reasonable measures to resolve genuine customer concerns. Excellent customer service 
strengthens the Company's reputation and supports customer retention, which is essential for sustainable growth in a competitive 
and liberalised financial environment.
 The Customer Grievance Cell (CGC) maintains an effective grievance redressal mechanism, which is integral to the growth and 
development of the Company. Root cause analyses are conducted to understand the nature of complaints received and to 
identify underlying causes, thereby facilitating systemic improvement. The Company accords the highest priority to meeting 
all applicable regulatory requirements.
 The Company's grievance redressal mechanism encompasses the following key steps:
  Complaint Registration: Complaints are received through multiple channels, including the Call Centre, branch offices, 
the Company's website, QR codes, feedback links, telephone, walk-in visits, and post. All complaints are registered in the 
Company's grievance system and managed by the Customer Grievance Cell (CGC).
  Immediate Action: The CGC provides support to customers and addresses their concerns in a timely and effective manner. 
All team members are trained to deliver a seamless and personalised customer experience.
  Customer Feedback: The Company regularly monitors customer feedback and takes prompt action to address customer 
needs. The CGC escalates grievances to the relevant departments to ensure timely resolution, supported by clear 
performance metrics.
 All grievances are addressed within 20 days of receipt. The CGC provides regular reports to senior management and leverages 
data analysis to derive actionable insights into customer behaviour, preferences, and emerging needs. Additional information is 
available on the Company's policy page under “Mechanism for Dealing with Customer Complaints and Redressal.”
